If <math>\text{P}</math>, <math>p</math> are the hydrostatic pressures in the liquid and vapour close to the meniscus, the difference <math>\text{P}-p=2\text{T}/r</math>. This is negative if <math>r</math> is negative, ''i.e.'' if the liquid rises in the tube, but is positive if the meniscus is convex and the liquid is depressed in the tube. If <math>\text{P}_0</math>, <math>p_0</math> are the pressures in the liquid and vapour at the plane surface, <math>\text{P}_0=p_0</math>, and if <math>1/\text{V}</math> is the density of the liquid, the differences of pressure in the liquid and vapour respectively corresponding to a difference of level <math>h</math>, are <math>\text{P}-\text{P}_0=-gh/\text{V}</math>, <math>p-p_0=-gh/v</math>. Combining these with the relation <math>\text{P}-p=2\text{T}/r</math> and eliminating <math>gh</math>, we obtain, for the change of vapour-pressure <math>p-p_0</math>, due to change of pressure <math>\text{P}-p_0</math>, or to curvature <math>1/r</math>,
{{block center|<math>p-p_0=(\text{P}-\text{P}_0)\text{V}/v=2\text{TV}/r(v-\text{V}).</math> . . . (2)}}

This increase of vapour-pressure with curvature affords a natural explanation of the fact that it is possible to cool a vapour considerably below the saturation temperature without condensation. The vapour-pressure in a fog containing small drops of radius <math>r</math> must exceed the normal vapour-pressure over a plane surface at the same temperature by the amount <math>2\text{TV}/r(v-\text{V})</math>, which may be considerable if <math>r</math> is small. The same expression measures the supersaturation required to induce condensation in the presence of dust or other nuclei of radius <math>r</math>, and explains why it is that condensation always takes place on dust particles if any are present. This phenomenon forms the basis of J. Aitken's method of counting dust particles, or Wilson's method of counting electrical ions, which are also capable of acting as nuclei for starting condensation.

7. ''Vapour-Pressure of Solutions.''—The rise of boiling-point produced by a substance in solution was demonstrated by M. Faraday in 1820, but the effect had been known to exist for a long time previously. C. H. L. Babo, 1847, gave the law known by his name, that the "relative lowering" <math>(p-p_0)/p_0</math> of the vapour-pressure of a solution, or the ratio of the diminution of vapour-pressure <math>(p-p_0)</math> to the vapour-pressure <math>p_0</math> of the pure solvent at the same temperature, was constant, or independent of the temperature, for any solution of constant strength. A. Wüllner (''Pogg. Ann.'' 1858, 103, p. 529) found the lowering of the vapour-pressure to be nearly proportional to the strength of the solution for the same salt. W. Ostwald, employing Wüllner's results, found the lowering of vapour-pressure produced by different salts in solution in water to be approximately the same for solutions containing the same number of gramme-molecules of salt per c.c. F. M. Raoult (''Comptes Rendus'', 1886–87) employed other solvents besides water, and showed that the relative lowering for different solvents and different dissolved substances was the same in many cases for solutions in which the ratio of the number of gramme-molecules <math>n</math> of the dissolved substance to the number of molecules <math>\text{N}</math> of the solvent was the same, or that it varied generally in proportion to the ratio <math>n/\text{N}</math>. The relative lowering of the vapour-pressure can be easily measured by Dalton's method of the barometer tube for solvents such as ether, which have

But in many cases it is more readily determined by observing the rise of the boiling-point or the depression of the freezing-point of the solution. For the rise in the boiling-point, we have by Clapeyron's equation, <math>dp/d\theta = \text{L}/\theta v</math>, nearly, neglecting the volume of the liquid as compared with that of the vapour <math>v</math>. If <math>dp</math> is the difference of vapour-pressure of solvent and solution, and <math>d\theta</math> the rise in the boiling-point, we have the approximate relation,
{{block center|<math>n/\text{N} = dp/p = m\text{L}d\theta/\text{R}\theta^2</math>, Raoult's law, . . (8)}}
where <math>m</math> is the molecular weight of the vapour, and R the gas-constant which is nearly 2 calories per degree for a gramme-molecule of gas. For the depression of the freezing-point a relation of the same form applies, but <math>d\theta</math> is negative, and L is the latent heat of fusion. At the freezing-point, the solution must have the same vapour-pressure as the solid solvent, with which it is in equilibrium. The relation follows immediately from Kirchhoff's expression (below, section 14) for the difference of vapour-pressure of the liquid and solid below the freezing-point.

''Extension to Higher Pressures.''—The approximate formula above given for the effect of hydrostatic pressure on the vapour-pressure assumes the densities of the liquid and vapour constant, and is true for small differences of pressure only. If we take <math>\text{P}_0</math> and <math>p_\theta</math> to represent corresponding values of the pressure in the liquid and vapour at the same level (and not necessarily at the plane surface where <math>\text{P}_0 = p_0</math>), and if the difference of level from <math>\text{P}</math>, <math>p</math> is small, substituting <math>d\text{P}</math> and <math>dp</math> for the small differences of pressure, we have accurately the relation <math>vdp = \text{V}d\text{P}</math>, where <math>\text{V}</math> and <math>v</math> are the specific volumes of the liquid and vapour under the pressures <math>\text{P}</math> and <math>p</math> respectively. In order to apply the formula to large differences of pressure, it is only necessary to integrate it at constant temperature between the required limits of <math>\text{P}</math> and <math>p</math>. We thus obtain the general equation,
{{block center|<math>\int_{p_0}^{p} vdp = \int_{\text{P}_0}^{\text{P}} \text{V}d\text{P}.</math> . . . . (3)}}

In applying the general equation (3) to an actual case, the compressibility of the liquid is the most uncertain factor. Assuming the compressibility constant, we may write <math>\text{V} = \text{V}_0(1 - a\text{P})</math>. For the vapour we may employ equation (17) {{sc|{{EB1911 article link|Thermodynamics}}}}, viz. <math>v = \text{R}\theta/p - c + b</math>, as a very close approximation over a wide range. The small quantities <math>c</math> and <math>b</math> are functions of the temperature only. Making these substitutions and integrating the equation we obtain
{{block center|<math>\text{R}\theta \log_e(p/p_0) = (c - b)(p - p_0) + \text{V}_0(\text{P} - \text{P}_0) - \tfrac{1}{2}a\text{V}_0(\text{P}^2 - \text{P}^2_0).</math> (4)}}

C. T. R. Wilson (''Phil. Trans.'' 1898) has observed that in the absence of nuclei a very fine mist is formed in a vapour on sudden expansion when its density is about eight times the saturation value. Putting <math>p/p_0 = 8</math> in equation (4), and taking for water vapour <math>\text{R} = 4{\cdot}61 \times 10^6</math>, and <math>\theta = 300^\circ</math> Abs. we find <math>\text{P} - \text{P}_0</math> equal to 3000 atmospheres approximately as the pressure required to produce this degree of supersaturation, allowing for compressibility of <math>\text{V}</math>. The term <math>(c - b)</math> may be neglected in this case, as <math>p</math> is small, but it would amount to about 17% of <math>\text{PV}</math> at 200° C. The result obtained from the approximate formula (2) would be 9200 atmospheres, which is more than treble, and indicates the inapplicability of the simple formula in an extreme case. Taking <math>\text{P} = 3000</math> atmospheres, and assuming that the formula <math>2\text{T}/r</math> applies for the capillary pressure, we find the equivalent radius of a nucleus corresponding to the fine misty condensation to be <math>5\cdot0\times10^{-8}</math> cm. 6. ''Application to a Solid.''—If we imagine a vertical column of solid in a porous vessel at uniform temperature surrounded by vapour, it would appear probable by similar reasoning that it would be in equilibrium under its own hydrostatic pressure with the pressure of the vapour at different levels. This would give the same formula as (2) for the variation of vapour-pressure, with <math>\text{V}'</math>, the specific volume of the solid, in place of <math>\text{V}</math>. But since the surface tension analogy does not exactly apply in the case of a solid, it is perhaps better to deduce the formula from a consideration of the effect of pressure on the freezing-point. The freezing-point <math>\theta_0</math> is the point at which the solid and liquid have the same vapour-pressure <math>p_0</math>. Otherwise they could not remain together in equilibrium. When the freezing-point is changed by pressure, the vapour-pressures <math>p'</math>, <math>p''</math>, of the solid and liquid must be the same at the new freezing-point. The rise of the freezing-point <math>\theta-\theta_0</math>, for an increase of pressure <math>\text{P}-\text{P}_0</math>, is given by the thermodynamic equation ({{sc|{{1911link|Thermodynamics}}}}, equation (5))
{{block center|<math>\text{L}(\theta-\theta_0)/\theta_0 = (\text{P}-\text{P}_0)(\text{V}''-\text{V}'),</math> . . . (5)}}
where <math>\text{L}</math> is the latent heat of fusion, and <math>\text{V}'</math>, <math>\text{V}''</math> are the specific volumes of the solid and liquid respectively. The difference <math>(p'-p'')</math> of the vapour-pressures of the solid and liquid under normal pressure <math>\text{P}_0</math> at a temperature <math>\theta</math> near the normal freezing-point <math>\theta_0</math>, is deduced from the same equation (see section 24 below)
{{block center|<math>p'-p'' = \text{L}(\theta-\theta_0)/v\theta_0,</math> . . . (6)}}
where <math>v</math> is the specific volume of the vapour. Substituting for <math>\theta</math> in terms of <math>\text{P}</math> from (5), we have for the difference of the vapour-pressures at <math>\theta_0</math> under pressure <math>\text{P}</math>,
{{block center|<math>p'-p'' = (\text{P}-\text{P}_0)\ (\text{V}''-\text{V}')/v.</math> . . . (7)}}
The increase of vapour-pressure of the liquid when the pressure is increased to <math>\text{P}</math> is given by (2), viz. <math>p''-p_0 = (\text{P}-\text{P}_0)\text{V}''/v</math>. The increase of vapour-pressure of the solid must be less than that of the liquid by the amount given by (7), in order that their vapour-pressure may be the same at the new freezing-point <math>\theta</math>. We thus obtain by subtraction
{{block center|<math>p'-p_0 = (\text{P}-\text{P}_0)\{\text{V}''/v-(\text{V}''-\text{V}')/v\} = (\text{P}-\text{P}_0)\text{V}'/v.</math>}} Which is precisely the same as relation (2) for the liquid, with <math>\text{V}'</math> substituted for <math>\text{V}''</math>. Hence the effect of pressure on the vapour-pressure follows the same law for both liquid and solid (J. H. Poynting, ''Phil. Mag.'' xii. p. 40, 1881).
